newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free seven, show no sign of surrender.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free seven, show no sign of surrender.

text.p: Marxist rebels inside the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima made another small guesture of conciliation on Wednesday, freeing seven hostages, but showed no sign of giving in to demands they end the 15-day-old standoff.
The New Year's Day releases continued the pattern of recent days during which the guerrillas have allowed a small number of captives to trickle out.

But the release did little to change the overall balance of the hostage crisis, with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels sticking to their original demand that the government pardon about 400 jailed comrades.

They still held 74 hostages whom they consider to be the most valuable -- including high-ranking government officials and military top brass, two foreign ambassadors and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.

The seven released on Wednesday were four Japanese businessmen and three Peruvians, including a top privatisation official, Juan Assereto. All of them appeared in good health as they strolled out of the Japanese ambassador's residence clutching plastic bags containing dirty clothes.

The releases followed a relatively quiet day after frantic activity on Tuesday, when the rebels released two diplomats and staged a massive publicity stunt by granting an impromptu news conference inside the residence.
Fujimori, apparently furious at the rebels' propaganda coup, stayed in his office at Government Palace with security advisers.
"He's annoyed and wouldn't you be? They took the initiative and made a mockery of him, managing to send their faces around the world in minutes," a palace source told Reuters.

Dressed in combat gear and carrying an automatic rifle, Nestor Cerpa, leader of the 20-odd rebels who stormed a lavish party at the residence on Dec. 17, held court for about two hours and harangued Fuijimori's "dictatorship".
Cerpa reiterated that the rebels would not surrender until their prisoners had been released and said he was in no hurry to end the standoff.
He added, however, that the doors of the residence were open to government negotiators and said he was willing to consider mediation by Cuba or Russia.
Fujimori has flatly rejected the rebel's demands and his chief negotiator in the crisis -- Education Minister Domingo Palermo -- stayed away from the diplomatic compound.
An MRTA spokesman told Reuters the rebels would sawp their hostages for the liberation of some of their jailed comrades.

"Our original and central demand is the release of comrades in jail, and an exchange of the prisoners of war is one obvious way to achieve this," MRTA member Isaac Velazco told Reuters in a telephone interview from Hamburg, Germany.

Wednesday's releases again coincided with the presence of Peruvian Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani at the residence. Diplomatic observers have speculated that Cipriani, a close personal friend of Fujimori, has taken on an important negotiating role in the crisis, something which Cipriani has publically denied.
Journalists who entered the Japanese compound on Tuesday described a home turned upside down in an effort to accomodate hundreds of unforeseen guests.
Furniture had been piled up against doors and windows as barricades and discarded litter and food covered the floor. The rebels have booby-trapped and mined the residence aganist possible attack.
Haggard-looking hostages paraded before the press by the guerrillas said they were being treated well and insisted the crisis must be ended peacefully.
While Fujimori maintained a rigid silence, the man whose birthday the ill-fated reception was celebrating, expressed his deep concern for the remaining hostages.
"My heart hurts deeply when I think of those who cannot celebrate the New Year with their families," Japanese Emperor Akihito was quoted as saying by Yomiuri Shimbun.
In Lima hundreds carrying flags and banners joined a peace march through the streets shouting, "Free the hostages! The people want peace!".
